summary: A 1970 memo presenting the new host-to-host protocol, with changes from the earlier design in RFC 11 that came out of a December 1969 network meeting. It was described as not yet detailed enough to write a network control program from. It was updated by RFC 36 and RFC 47.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes an early design for programs on different ARPA Network computers to communicate. It sketches message delivery, process connections, and the Network Control Program, while warning that the description is not yet complete enough to implement an NCP.

subtitle: An early proposal for connections and process communication across the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network connected different host computers, so their operating systems needed a shared way to exchange messages and connect processes.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal describes messages sent through IMPs, logical links controlled by RFNM signals, and host-side NCPs that establish process connections using socket names.
tldr.outcome: The memo presents a developing design and says it does not contain enough information to write an NCP. Unit metadata lists later updates by RFC 36 and RFC 47.

today: RFC 33 is an early host-host protocol proposal, and the unit metadata lists RFC 36 and RFC 47 as updates to it.

sections.title: A Network of Different Hosts
sections.content:
The ARPA Network joined computers with different hardware and operating systems, with no single host controlling the others. The authors describe the network as a way for computers to send messages to other computers and to make remote resources available to users.

This RFC attaches a paper describing changes to an earlier host-host protocol. Its opening note says the document is incomplete for implementation and invites comments.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers needed a common way to exchange data without giving one computer control of the network. This memo outlines a design, but it is not a complete implementation guide.

sections.title: Messages, Links, and Flow Control
sections.content:
A host sends a message to its Interface Message Processor (IMP), which carries it toward another host. A message begins with a 32-bit leader containing the destination or sender host, message type, flags, and link number.

Each link is one-way, and the network allows only one message at a time on a link. After the message reaches the receiving host, an RFNM (Request-for-Next-Message) returns to the sender and permits another message on that link.
sections.plainLanguage: A message starts with a short header that identifies its route and logical link. The sender waits for an RFNM signal before sending another message on that same link.

sections.title: Connecting Processes with Sockets
sections.content:
A Network Control Program (NCP) on each host establishes, switches, and closes connections for local processes. A connection joins a sending process to a receiving process; two connections are needed for conversation in both directions.

Each endpoint is named by a socket made from a 24-bit user number, an 8-bit host number, and an 8-bit AEN. The host NCPs exchange control commands over a designated control link to request and accept connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs use their host's NCP to open a connection to another program. A socket name identifies each end, and the two NCPs agree on the connection.

sections.title: Managing Data and Remote Use
sections.content:
The proposal includes commands to initiate, accept, and close connections, and to send or receive messages. If a receiving host is running out of buffer space, it can send CEASE to stop further messages on a link and RESUME when sending can continue.

The memo also discusses remote login, TELNET use, and possible higher-level tools for interactive programs. It notes that a proposed Network Interface Language was not fully specified and that some host-to-IMP scheduling problems remained.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP can pause a sender when the receiving host needs time to handle queued data. The memo also explores remote login and interactive use, while identifying parts of the design that still needed work.
